full_title: BANCO MAXIMO, INC., PETITIONER, VS. CHRIS ANGELO C. PELAYO, MARY ANN C. PELAYO-CALISURA, AND CATHERINE C. PELAYO-SOCO, RESPONDENTS.
subject: Civil Law and Land Titles and Deeds
syllabus_topic: III. Family Relations > B. Family Relations > 5. Family Home
topics: Family home exemption must be timely and properly asserted
Exemption is a personal privilege; heirs who waived their interest lack standing
Family home not exempt from debts secured by a mortgage on the premises (Art. 155(3), Family Code)
A judgment on issues not raised in the pleadings is void
Rule 45: conflicting RTC and CA findings as an exception

other_subjects.subject: Remedial Law, Legal and Judicial Ethics
other_subjects.syllabus_topic: III. Civil Procedure > S. Post-judgment Remedies > 5. Appeal and Review > e. Modes > v. Appeal by Certiorari to SC (Rule 45)

doctrine:
A family home is the dwelling house where the spouses, or an unmarried head of a family, and their family reside, together with the land on which it stands. It is deemed constituted from the time it is occupied as a family residence, and it is generally exempt from execution, forced sale or attachment (Articles 152 and 153, Family Code). **But the exemption is not automatic: it must be timely and properly asserted by the proper party.** The claim must be set up and proved to the sheriff before the public auction (*Honrado v. Court of Appeals*; *Taruc v. Maximo*), or at the latest within a reasonable time, that is, before the one-year redemption period expires (*Spouses Fortaleza v. Spouses Lapitan*). Failure to do so estops the claimant. The Court reiterated these rules.

**The right to claim the exemption is a personal privilege.** Heirs who, through a voluntary extrajudicial settlement, waived all their interest in the property in favor of a co-heir before he mortgaged it have no standing to invoke the family home exemption to annul the mortgage and foreclosure. This is especially so when they raise it only after the auction and after failed attempts to redeem. A mortgagee bank that lent in good faith, relying on a tax declaration in the mortgagor's name and without notice of any adverse claim, is protected.

In any event, **under Article 155(3) of the Family Code, a family home is not exempt from execution for debts secured by mortgages on the premises, whether constituted before or after the family home.** A property's character as a family home does not by itself invalidate a mortgage or a foreclosure conducted in accordance with law. On procedure: when a court annuls a deed (here, the extrajudicial settlement) whose nullity no party alleged or prayed for, its judgment goes beyond the pleadings and is "extrajudicial and void."
facts:
Spouses Edgar and Marlinda Pelayo raised their four children in their house and lot in Barangay Nailon, Bogo City, Cebu. The children are respondents Chris Angelo, Mary Ann and Catherine (Chris et al.) and their brother Ian. Edgar died on January 10, 2004. On March 31, 2008, Marlinda and Chris et al. executed an Extrajudicial Declaration of Heirs with Waiver of Rights (EJS) waiving their interest in the property in favor of Ian, and a tax declaration was issued in Ian's name.

On December 3, 2008, Marlinda, as Ian's attorney-in-fact, obtained a PHP 400,000.00 loan from Banco Maximo, Inc., secured by a real estate mortgage over the property dated December 23, 2008. Ian defaulted, and the bank extrajudicially foreclosed. At the auction on January 24, 2012, the bank was the highest bidder at PHP 353,666.66, the unpaid principal. In October 2012, Chris et al. offered to redeem the property for PHP 500,000.00. The bank counter-offered PHP 800,000.00, and the negotiations failed.

On January 14, 2013, Chris et al. sued to annul the mortgage, the foreclosure sale and the certificate of sale, claiming that the property was a family home exempt from execution. The RTC dismissed the complaint. It held that Chris et al. had no standing because they were neither the owners of the property nor parties to the mortgage. It also held that there was no family home to speak of, because the lot belonged exclusively to Ian, and that the 10-year continuation under Article 159 did not apply because there were no minor beneficiaries.

The CA reversed on October 14, 2020. It held that the property remained a family home for 10 years after Edgar's death under Article 159 of the Family Code, so the 2008 partition through the EJS was invalid. It declared the mortgage, the foreclosure sale and the certificate of sale void. The CA denied reconsideration on April 22, 2021, and the bank filed a Rule 45 petition. Respondents filed no comment despite two directives from the Court.
issues: Whether the Court may review the factual question of whether the property is a family home in a Rule 45 petition.
Whether the CA erred in nullifying the real estate mortgage and the extrajudicial foreclosure on the ground that the property is a family home exempt from execution.
ruling:
As a preliminary matter, respondents' failure to comment despite repeated directives did not prevent the Court from resolving the case on the pleadings and the evidence on record.

**1. Yes.** Only questions of law may be raised under Rule 45, and the issues here were essentially factual. But a conflict between the findings of the RTC and the CA is a recognized exception. The RTC found that the property ceased to be a family home after Edgar's death and the EJS; the CA held that it remained one. These divergent views required the Court's intervention.

**2. Yes, the CA erred.** A family home is deemed constituted from the time it is occupied as a family residence, and it is generally exempt from execution, forced sale or attachment (Articles 152 and 153, Family Code). **However, "this exemption is not automatic and must be timely and properly asserted."** Under *Honrado v. Court of Appeals*, the claim "should be set up and proved to the Sheriff before the sale of the property at public auction," and failure to do so estops the party from claiming it later. *Taruc v. Maximo* reiterated that the exemption must be asserted before the auction. *Spouses Fortaleza v. Spouses Lapitan* held that it must be asserted within a reasonable time, that is, before the one-year redemption period expires. **The right to claim the exemption "is a personal privilege, and may only be invoked by the proper party."**

Respondents had no standing to invoke it. Through their own voluntary EJS, they waived all their interest in favor of Ian before the mortgage was executed, and they did not assert the exemption before the auction. They first tried to redeem the property, which implicitly recognized the mortgage and the foreclosure. They raised the family home claim only after the negotiations failed and title was consolidated in the bank, which suggests it was "merely an afterthought." Letting them prevail would also be unjust to the bank. It extended credit in good faith on the strength of a tax declaration showing Ian as the owner, with no notice of any adverse claim. A ruling for respondents would "embolden parties to renege on contractual obligations" and erode confidence in secured transactions.

The CA also declared the EJS void even though no one alleged or prayed for its annulment. It thus resolved an issue never raised and disregarded respondents' express waiver in favor of Ian. A judgment that goes beyond the pleadings "is not merely irregular, but extrajudicial and void" (*Bernas v. Court of Appeals*).

**Finally, even if the property remained a family home despite the EJS, the mortgage and the foreclosure stand. Under Article 155 of the Family Code, a family home is not exempt from execution for debts secured by mortgages on the premises, whether constituted before or after the family home.** Being a family home does not by itself invalidate a mortgage or a foreclosure conducted in accordance with law.
disposition: The Petition for Review on Certiorari was GRANTED. The CA Decision dated October 14, 2020 and Resolution dated April 22, 2021 in CA-G.R. CEB CV No. 07144 were REVERSED and SET ASIDE. The Decision dated February 29, 2016 of the RTC, Branch 61, Bogo City, Cebu in Civil Case No. Bogo-02891, which dismissed respondents' complaint, was REINSTATED.

bar_questions.q: After their father died, siblings Rina, Sonny and Tess, together with their mother, executed an extrajudicial settlement waiving all their rights over the family's house and lot in favor of their brother Udo. A tax declaration was issued in Udo's name. Udo then mortgaged the property to XYZ Bank to secure a loan. When Udo defaulted, the bank extrajudicially foreclosed and bought the property at the auction. No one claimed any exemption before the sale. After failed negotiations to redeem the property and the consolidation of title in the bank, Rina, Sonny and Tess sued to annul the mortgage and the foreclosure, arguing that the property is their family home and is therefore exempt from forced sale. Will the action prosper?

alac.answer: No. The siblings cannot invoke the family home exemption to annul the mortgage and the foreclosure.
alac.legal_basis: A family home is generally exempt from execution, forced sale or attachment (Articles 152 and 153, Family Code). But the exemption is not automatic. It must be timely and properly asserted, by setting it up and proving it to the sheriff before the auction, or at the latest before the redemption period expires. It is a personal privilege that only the proper party may invoke. Moreover, under Article 155(3) of the Family Code, a family home is not exempt for debts secured by mortgages on the premises. (Banco Maximo, Inc. v. Pelayo, G.R. No. 257251, August 18, 2025, citing Honrado v. Court of Appeals and Spouses Fortaleza v. Spouses Lapitan)
alac.application: The siblings voluntarily waived all their interest in Udo's favor before the mortgage, so they are not the proper parties to claim the exemption. They did not assert it before the auction, and they first tried to redeem the property, which implicitly recognized the mortgage and the foreclosure. Their claim, raised only after title was consolidated, is a belated afterthought. The bank lent in good faith, relying on a tax declaration in Udo's name and without notice of any adverse claim. Finally, the debt was secured by a mortgage on the very property, so even a valid family home would not be exempt from foreclosure.
alac.conclusion: The action will not prosper, and the mortgage and the foreclosure remain valid.

bar_questions.q: Vic, a widower, lives with his two minor children in a house and lot he owns, which has been their family residence since 2015. Its value is within the limit allowed by law. In 2022, he borrowed money from Wally without giving any security. Wally obtained a money judgment against Vic, and the sheriff levied on the house and lot. (a) Before the scheduled auction, Vic filed a claim with the sheriff that the property is a family home, with proof that his family has lived there since 2015. Should the claim be recognized? (b) Would your answer be the same if Vic had secured the 2022 loan with a real estate mortgage on the house and lot, and Wally foreclosed the mortgage?

alac.answer: (a) Yes. Vic timely and properly asserted the exemption. (b) No. A family home is not exempt from foreclosure for a debt secured by a mortgage on it.
alac.legal_basis: A family home is deemed constituted from the time it is occupied as a family residence. As long as any of its beneficiaries actually resides there, it is exempt from execution, forced sale or attachment, to the extent of the value allowed by law. The exceptions include debts incurred before its constitution and debts secured by mortgages on the premises, whether before or after its constitution (Articles 152, 153 and 155, Family Code). The exemption must be timely and properly asserted by the proper party, that is, set up and proved to the sheriff before the auction. (Banco Maximo, Inc. v. Pelayo, G.R. No. 257251, August 18, 2025)
alac.application: (a) The house became a family home in 2015, when Vic and his children began living there, and they still live there. The 2022 debt was incurred after the family home was constituted and is unsecured, so no exception under Article 155 applies. Vic, the owner and head of the family living in the house, is the proper party, and he raised the claim with proof before the auction. Unlike the heirs in Banco Maximo, he did not waive his interest or wait until after the sale. (b) If the loan was secured by a mortgage on the property, Article 155(3) applies. The property's character as a family home would not invalidate the mortgage or the foreclosure.
alac.conclusion: Vic's timely claim protects the family home against the unsecured judgment debt, but not against foreclosure of a mortgage he constituted on it.

bar_questions.q: Celia sued to annul a real estate mortgage and the foreclosure sale of a lot, alleging only that the mortgage was void. She did not question the deed of sale by which the mortgagor had earlier acquired the lot from her, and she did not ask for its annulment. The RTC dismissed the complaint. On appeal, the CA, making factual findings contrary to the RTC's, declared void the deed of sale, the mortgage and the foreclosure. The mortgagee bank filed a petition for review on certiorari under Rule 45 with the Supreme Court. (a) May the Supreme Court review the CA's factual findings? (b) Did the CA validly annul the deed of sale?

alac.answer: (a) Yes. A conflict between the factual findings of the RTC and the CA is a recognized exception to the rule that only questions of law may be raised under Rule 45. (b) No. The CA could not annul a deed whose validity was never put in issue.
alac.legal_basis: Under Rule 45, only questions of law may be raised, but the Court may review factual issues when the findings of the RTC and the CA conflict. Courts have no jurisdiction or power to decide a question not in issue. A judgment that goes beyond the pleadings and adjudicates matters on which the parties were not heard "is not merely irregular, but extrajudicial and void" (Bernas v. Court of Appeals, applied in Banco Maximo, Inc. v. Pelayo, G.R. No. 257251, August 18, 2025).
alac.application: (a) The RTC and the CA reached opposite conclusions on the facts, so the Supreme Court may examine the evidence to resolve the conflict. (b) Celia's complaint attacked only the mortgage and the foreclosure. She never alleged that the deed of sale was void or asked for its annulment, and the bank was never heard on it. By annulling the deed, the CA decided an issue outside the pleadings, so that part of its judgment is void. Banco Maximo is on point: there, the CA annulled an extrajudicial settlement that no party had challenged.
alac.conclusion: The Supreme Court may review the conflicting factual findings, and it should set aside the CA's annulment of the unchallenged deed of sale.

notes: The narrative gives the RTC decision date as February 19, 2016, but the CA fallo, the Supreme Court fallo and footnote 4 give February 29, 2016; the disposition uses February 29, 2016. The Supreme Court did not rule on the CA's reading of Article 159 (the family home continues for 10 years after a spouse's death, and the heirs cannot partition it), nor on the RTC's view that Article 159 requires a minor beneficiary. It held instead that, even if the property remained a family home, Article 155(3) defeats the claim. The text's "SO ORDERED." line carries a stray closing quotation mark.
